biography:
Samuel 'Smith' Sterling earned his nickname the old-fashioned way—by spending so much time at his forge that people forgot his given name existed. Born on a frontier mining station where quality equipment was either imported at exorbitant cost or cobbled together from scrap, Samuel watched miners die regularly because their tools failed under pressure. He became obsessed with the idea that good tools should be affordable and reliable, that craftsmanship serves people rather than impresses them. Samuel opened a mobile workshop, traveling between stations to offer repairs and custom equipment at prices working miners could actually afford. His designs aren't pretty—they're functional, durable, and repairable with common parts—but they've saved countless miners from dangerous situations when corporate equipment would have failed. Other craftsmen look down on Samuel's work as crude or utilitarian, but the miners who depend on his tools know better. Samuel doesn't care about fame or artistry; he cares about whether his tools keep people alive when it matters.

Smith speaks with the blunt, practical tones of someone who's always thinking about the problem at hand and has zero patience for pretension. He has the rough working-class accent of the frontier stations, and his speech is filled with practical observations, mechanical references, and dismissive comments about fancy designs that don't work in real conditions. He's friendly enough, but he gets frustrated quickly when people prioritize aesthetics over function, and he's been known to throw customers out of his workshop when they ask for decorative features. When building or repairing equipment, he sounds like someone explaining something obvious to a particularly slow child: 'Look, I don't care if it matches your ship's color scheme. I care about whether it holds together when the pressure spikes and the temperature drops. This design—this ugly, boring design—has worked in these conditions for fifty years. You want something fancy? Go talk to Arthur Artificer. He'll make you something beautiful that'll fail the first time things get difficult. You want something that works? Let me finish this, and you can pick it up tomorrow. Cash only—I don't take credit from people who don't understand what matters.'
name: Samuel 'Smith' Sterling
